segments.text: In the last topic, we established what an AI agent is.
A system that doesn't just respond but acts.
We introduced Solara Energy and looked at how agents can take a goal like monitoring site
performance and turn it into a sequence of real actions, querying data, comparing outputs,
flagging anomalies, and generating reports.
But not all agents work the same way.
There are different types built on different architectures designed for different kinds of problems.
And understanding those differences is what allows you to match the right agent to the right job.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to describe the core components that make up an AI
agent's architecture, explain how agents interact with their environment through a continuous loop,
walk through the perception reasoning action cycle that drives
agent decision-making, and identify the three main types of agents and when each is appropriate,
as well as visualize how a complete agent workflow flows from input to outcome.
Let's start with what's inside.
Every AI agent, regardless of type, is built from the same fundamental components.
There's the perception layer. This is how the agent receives information from the world around it.
At Solara, that might mean reading an incoming data feed from a solar installation,
receiving a user query, or picking up a trigger from a monitoring system.
There's the memory layer. As we covered in the last topic, agents hold short-term context
within a task and can access long-term memory from external storage. This is what allows an
agent to reason across multiple steps without losing track of where it is.
There's the reasoning engine, the LLM, which interprets what the agent has perceived,
decides what to do next, and determines which tools to use.
And there's the action layer. This is where the agent does something in the world,
runs a query, calls an API, writes a file, sends an alert.
These four components work together in a continuous loop. The agent perceives,
reasons, acts, then perceives again based on the result of that action.
That loop is what we call agent-environment interaction. And it's worth understanding
because it's what separates an agent from a static tool.
A static tool waits to be asked. An agent operates within an environment. It observes
what's happening, decides what action is appropriate, and executes. Then it checks
the result and decides what comes next. At Solara, an agent monitoring grid performance
isn't just waiting for someone to run a report. It's watching. When output at a site drops below
threshold, it observes the deviation, decides the appropriate response, which might be querying
historical data, cross-referencing weather records, or escalating to a human operator,
and takes that action. The environment shapes the agent. The agent shapes the environment.
That bi-directional relationship is what makes agents useful in dynamic, real-world data context.
Let's slow that loop down and look at each stage. Perception is input. The agent receives
information, a data reading, a user request, a tool result, an error message. It takes that in
and adds it to its working context. Reasoning is interpretation and planning. The agent's
LLM process is what it's received, considers its goal, reviews what it's already done,
and decides what action to take next. This is where the intelligence lives.
Action is execution. The agent calls a tool, writes an output, sends a message,
or updates a record. Something changes in the world as a result. Then the cycle begins again.
The result of the action becomes new perception. The agent reasons about what that result means.
For Solara's equipment health monitoring agent, this cycle might run dozens of times
in a single task. Querying data, evaluating results, deciding what to check next,
generating a finding before it produces a final output. Now let's talk about the three main types
of agents because not every problem needs the same architecture. The first type is the reactive agent.
A reactive agent responds to its current input using predefined rules. It has no memory of what
happened before, no ability to plan ahead. It simply observes a condition and responds.
Think of a simple alert agent at Solara. If output at site 12 drops below 8% of a baseline,
send a notification. That's a reactive agent. Fast, predictable, easy to build, but limited.
It can't investigate why the drop happened or determine whether the alert is actually worth
sending. The second type is the goal-based agent. A goal-based agent reasons about actions
in terms of whether they move it closer to a defined outcome. It plans and evaluates options.
It chooses the path most likely to achieve the goal. Solara's site performance investigation
agent works this way. Its goal is to determine why Site 47 underperformed last Tuesday. It
doesn't follow a fixed script. It decides what data to pull based on what it finds,
adjusting its approach as results come in. The third type is the utility-based agent.
A utility-based agent goes further than goal-based reasoning. It doesn't just ask,
will this action achieve the goal. It asks, which available action achieves the goal
most efficiently at the lowest cost and with the highest confidence. At Solara,
a utility-based agent managing report generation across hundreds of sites needs to make trade-off
decisions constantly. Do I generate a full diagnostic report or a summary? Do I escalate
this anomaly or log it for review? It evaluates options against a utility function and picks
the best one. Let's zoom out and look at how these components and concepts come together
in a complete agent workflow. A goal arrives. The agent perceives it, adds it to context and begins
reasoning. It identifies the first action needed and executes. The results come back,
the agent evaluates whether it's closer to the goal, it plans the next action,
it executes again. This continues, perceive, reason, act. Until the goal is reached,
an error condition is triggered or the agent determines it cannot proceed and hands off to a human.
What's important to notice is that workflow is the handoff point. Good agent design always includes
a point at which the agent recognizes the limits of its confidence and escalates. That's
an equipment anomaly it can't fully explain and routes it to a human engineer isn't falling short.
It's doing exactly what it should. Let's bring it together. Every agent is built from four components
perception, memory, reasoning and action working together in a continuous loop. That loop drives
agent environment interaction. The agent observes, decides, acts and observes again.
The three types of agents, reactive, goal-based and utility-based, represent increasing levels
of sophistication. Reactive agents are fast and rule-driven. Goal-based agents plan towards
outcomes. Utility-based agents optimize across trade-offs. Coming up next, we're going hands
on. In the demo, we'll visualize types and architectures of AI agents in action so you can see the
decision loops and execution patterns we've been discussing actually running in real time. Let's
take a look.
